query: FeCoNi is an fcc alloy with high saturation magnetization and a low coercive field. Earlier studies examined the high-entropy alloys FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt, but both exhibited soft ferromagnetism. A qualifying high-entropy alloy must have an almost equiatomic multicomponent composition and configurational entropy of at least 1.0R. Subject to these constraints, what single intervention could produce a FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy with greater coercivity than the prior derivatives? Present one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to an appropriate FeCoNi-based baseline, defines the conditions over which it should apply, cites supporting observations from earlier work, and proposes a discriminating experiment with an explicit falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Interstitial nitrogen doping can increase the coercivity of an equiatomic FeCoNi high-entropy alloy by inducing lattice distortions that enhance domain wall pinning.
generation.material_initial_state: An equiatomic, disordered FeCoNi alloy with an FCC crystal structure exhibiting high saturation magnetization and low coercivity.
generation.intervention: Introduce a low concentration (≈0.5 at.%) of interstitial nitrogen into the FeCoNi matrix.
generation.conditions: The alloy must remain equiatomic among the metals to maintain a configurational entropy of at least 1.0R, and the nitrogen concentration should be kept within the solubility limit to achieve uniform interstitial occupation in a face‐centered cubic lattice at room temperature.
generation.structural_mediator: Interstitial nitrogen atoms causing local lattice distortions and an increase in the stacking fault energy.
generation.mechanism: Nitrogen incorporation increases the stacking fault energy of the FCC matrix, as observed in similar CoCrNi systems. This change can modify the dislocation behavior and limit twin formation, leading to a more distorted lattice that enhances domain wall pinning. Strong pinning sites impede the movement of domain walls during magnetization reversal, thereby increasing the coercive field.
generation.predicted_outcome: The nitrogen-doped FeCoNi alloy will exhibit a higher coercivity than the previously studied soft ferromagnetic FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt alloys, while retaining high saturation magnetization.
generation.baseline: FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloys such as FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt, which have shown soft ferromagnetism with low coercivity.
generation.boundary: Effectiveness may be sensitive to the precise nitrogen content and the processing conditions; too high a nitrogen content could lead to the formation of unwanted phases or precipitates that might compromise the desired magnetic properties.
generation.uncertainty: While the increased stacking fault energy via interstitial nitrogen has been demonstrated in similar FCC systems (e.g., CoCrNi alloys), its exact influence on magnetic coercivity through domain wall pinning in FeCoNi remains to be directly measured and may depend on additional microstructural factors.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sample sets: one baseline equiatomic FeCoNi alloy and one identical alloy doped with ≈0.5 at.% nitrogen. Use methods such as gas-phase nitridation or nitrogen ion implantation to introduce nitrogen uniformly under controlled conditions. Ensure that both alloys are processed similarly to isolate the effect of interstitial nitrogen. Characterize the phase, composition, and microstructure using X-ray diffraction, electron microscopy, and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy.
measurements: Magnetic hysteresis loops to measure coercivity and saturation magnetization
Microstructural analysis to confirm interstitial nitrogen incorporation and assess lattice distortions
Stacking fault energy estimations via electron microscopy or diffraction techniques
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nitrogen-doped FeCoNi alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant increase (e.g., ≥10% higher) in coercive field compared to the baseline alloy, or if undesirable phases form that adversely affect the magnetic properties, the hypothesis would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
## Abstract
ABSTRACTWe investigated the effects of interstitial N and C on the stacking fault energy (SFE) of an equiatomic CoCrNi medium entropy alloy. Results of computer modeling were compared to tensile deformation and electron microscopy data. Both N and C in solid solution increase the SFE of the face-centered cubic (FCC) alloy matrix at room temperature, with the former having a more significant effect by 240% for 0.5 at % N. Total energy calculations based on density functional theory (DFT) as well as thermodynamic modeling of the Gibbs free energy with the CALPHAD (CALculation of PHAse Diagrams) method reveal a stabilizing effect of N and C interstitials on the FCC lattice with respect to the hexagonal close-packed (HCP) CoCrNi-X (X: N, C) lattice. Scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) measurements of the width of dissociated ½<110> dislocations suggest that the SFE of CoCrNi increases from 22 to 42–44 mJ·m−2 after doping the alloy with 0.5 at. % interstitial N. The higher SFE reduces the nucleation rates of twins, leading to an increase in the critical stress required to trigger deformation twinning, an effect which can be used to design load-dependent strain h
